title: A Tiny Lab Universe Where Time Emerged on Its Own
hook: What if time isn't a built-in feature of the universe, but something that emerges from change itself? A physicist built a 24,000-atom 'mini universe' with no external clock — and time appeared anyway.
key_points: University of Birmingham physicist Giovanni Barontini split 24,000 ultracold atoms into an 'observed' and 'unobserved' region using two laser beams.
With no external clock, time instead emerged from entropy: as atoms redistributed between the two regions, the system moved forward in what Barontini calls 'entropic time.'
When the atom distribution stopped changing, time effectively came to a halt in the system.
The result supports the idea, tied to the Wheeler-DeWitt equation, that time isn't fundamental but emerges from relationships between a system's parts.
content_html: Physics normally treats time as a given: a clock ticks somewhere outside the system you're studying, and everything else evolves relative to it. But what if there's no clock at all? University of Birmingham physicist Giovanni Barontini built a stripped-down quantum system to find out.
extra_html: His setup used 24,000 ultracold atoms, chilled to billionths of a degree above absolute zero, split by two laser beams of different frequencies into a "bright," observed region and a "dark," unobserved region inside an isolated chamber — with no external clock feeding the system any information about time. Instead, time emerged from entropy: as atoms redistributed between the bright and dark regions, the system moved forward in what Barontini calls "entropic time." When the atom distribution stopped changing, time in the system effectively came to a halt. The result is consistent with ideas tied to the Wheeler-DeWitt equation in quantum gravity, which suggests time isn't a built-in feature of the universe at all, but something that emerges from relationships between a system's own components. Barontini's team also showed the Schrödinger equation can be reformulated using this entropic time and still describe quantum mechanics consistently. Published in Physical Review Research.

related.title: Physicists Made a Quantum System's Arrow of Time Run Backward
related.hook: By carefully steering quantum measurements, researchers made a system behave as if time were flowing in reverse — and found they could harvest energy from the trick itself.

related.title: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle
related.hook: Nature sets a hard limit: the more precisely you know where a particle is, the less you can know about how it's moving. It's not sloppy measurement — it's built into reality.

related.title: The Fifth State of Matter, Made in Space
related.hook: Chill a gas to a hair above absolute zero and its atoms stop acting like a crowd and merge into one quantum entity. In orbit, weightlessness lets that strange state last even longer.

flashcards.prompt: How was this 'mini universe' built, and why does it matter that it had no external clock?
flashcards.back_html: From 24,000 ultracold atoms split by lasers into an 'observed' and 'unobserved' region, with no clock feeding the system a sense of time from outside.

flashcards.prompt: Where did time 'come from' in this experiment, since there was no external clock?

choices.text: From entropy changes, as atoms redistributed between the two regions — 'entropic time'
From a hidden atomic clock built into the apparatus
Time didn't actually pass in the experiment at all

flashcards.explanation_html: Barontini calls this 'entropic time': the system's forward progress tracked how the atom distribution changed, not any external timekeeper.

flashcards.prompt: What happened to time in the system once the atom distribution stopped changing?
flashcards.back_html: Time effectively came to a halt — with nothing left to change, there was nothing left to mark time's passage.

flashcards.prompt: What broader idea about time does this experiment lend support to?

choices.text: That time isn't a fundamental feature of the universe, but emerges from relationships between a system's parts
That time flows at the same rate everywhere in the universe, always
That quantum mechanics requires an external clock to work at all

flashcards.explanation_html: This connects to the Wheeler-DeWitt equation, which suggests time may not be built into the universe's fundamental description — it can emerge instead.
